claim: Numerous anti-cancer drugs perturb thymidylate biosynthesis and lead to genomic uracil incorporation contributing to their antiproliferative effect.
source: Numerous anti-cancer drugs perturb thymidylate biosynthesis and lead to genomic uracil incorporation contributing to their antiproliferative effect.
evidence: This is a general statement about anti-cancer drugs and their mechanism, drawing from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: A straightforward U-DNA sequencing method (U-DNA-Seq) was developed.
source: We developed a straightforward U-DNA sequencing method (U-DNA-Seq) that was combined with in situ super-resolution imaging.
evidence: The manuscript describes the development and application of this new method.

claim: A novel robust analysis pipeline was developed for U-DNA-Seq data.
source: Using a novel robust analysis pipeline, we found broad regions with elevated probability of uracil occurrence both in treated and non-treated cells.
evidence: The manuscript describes the development and application of this computational pipeline.

claim: Broad regions with elevated probability of uracil occurrence were found in both treated and non-treated cells.
source: Using a novel robust analysis pipeline, we found broad regions with elevated probability of uracil occurrence both in treated and non-treated cells.
evidence: This finding is based on the U-DNA-Seq data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Non-treated cells possess uracil in the late replicating constitutive heterochromatic regions.
source: Correlation with chromatin markers and other genomic features shows that non-treated cells possess uracil in the late replicating constitutive heterochromatic regions, while drug treatment induced a shift of incorporated uracil towards segments that are normally more active/functional.
evidence: This conclusion is based on correlation analysis of U-DNA-Seq data with chromatin markers and genomic features.

claim: Drug treatment induced a shift of incorporated uracil towards segments that are normally more active/functional.
source: Correlation with chromatin markers and other genomic features shows that non-treated cells possess uracil in the late replicating constitutive heterochromatic regions, while drug treatment induced a shift of incorporated uracil towards segments that are normally more active/functional.
evidence: This conclusion is based on correlation analysis of U-DNA-Seq data with chromatin markers and genomic features.

claim: Uracil is one of the most frequent non-canonical bases in DNA.
source: The thymine analogue uracil is one of the most frequent non-canonical bases in DNA appearing either by thymine replacing misincorporation or as a product of spontaneous or enzymatic cytosine deamination reaction (Krokan et al., 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Krokan et al., 2002.

claim: Uracil in DNA appears either by thymine replacing misincorporation or as a product of spontaneous or enzymatic cytosine deamination reaction.
source: The thymine analogue uracil is one of the most frequent non-canonical bases in DNA appearing either by thymine replacing misincorporation or as a product of spontaneous or enzymatic cytosine deamination reaction (Krokan et al., 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Krokan et al., 2002.

claim: Uracil in DNA is usually recognized as an error that is efficiently repaired by the multistep base excision repair (BER) pathway initiated by uracil-DNA glycosylases (UDGs).
source: Consequently, uracil in DNA is usually recognized as an error that is efficiently repaired by the multistep base excision repair (BER) pathway initiated by uracil-DNA glycosylases (UDGs) (Krokan and Bjørås, 2013; Wallace, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Krokan and Bjørås, 2013 and Wallace, 2014.

claim: Uracil in DNA is known to be involved in several physiological processes including antibody maturation, antiviral response, and insect development.
source: In other respects, uracil in DNA is known to be involved in several physiological processes (e.g. antibody maturation [Liu and Schatz, 2009; Maul and Gearhart, 2010; Maul and Gearhart, 2014; Xu et al., 2012], antiviral response [Burns et al., 2015; Stenglein et al., 2010], insect development [Horváth et al., 2013; Muha et al., 2012]), however, the exact mechanism and regulation of uracil-DNA metabolism including the roles of UDGs need to be elucidated.
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: There are four known members of the UDG family in humans: UNG, SMUG1, TDG, and MBD4.
source: There are four known members of the UDG family in humans: (i) the most active uracil-DNA glycosylase encoded by the ung gene (UNG1 mitochondrial and UNG2 nuclear isoform), (ii) the single-strand selective monofunctional uracil-DNA glycosylase 1 (SMUG1), (iii) thymine DNA glycosylase (TDG specialized for repair of T:G and U:G) and (iv) methyl CpG binding domain protein 4 (MBD4 repairs U:G) (Visnes et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Visnes et al., 2009.

claim: UNG2 removes most of the genomic uracil from both single- and double-stranded DNA regardless of the uracil originating from mutagenic cytosine deamination or thymine replacing misincorporation.
source: UNG2 removes most of the genomic uracil from both single- and double-stranded DNA regardless of the uracil originating from mutagenic cytosine deamination or thymine replacing misincorporation (Kavli et al., 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Kavli et al., 2002.

claim: Thymine replacing uracil misincorporation is normally prevented by the tight regulation of the cellular dUTP/dTTP ratio maintained by dUTPase and thymidylate synthase.
source: Thymine replacing uracil misincorporation is normally prevented by the tight regulation of the cellular dUTP/dTTP ratio maintained by two enzymes, the dUTPase and the thymidylate synthase.
evidence: This is a statement about cellular regulation mechanisms, drawing from established knowledge.

claim: The dUTPase enzyme removes dUTP from the cellular pool by catalyzing dUTP hydrolysis into dUMP and PPi.
source: The dUTPase enzyme removes dUTP from the cellular pool by catalyzing dUTP hydrolysis into dUMP and PPi (Vértessy and Tóth, 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Vértessy and Tóth, 2009.

claim: Lack or inhibition of dUTPase leads to increased dUTP levels and DNA polymerases readily incorporate uracil opposite to adenine.
source: Lack or inhibition of dUTPase leads to increased dUTP levels and under such conditions, DNA polymerases readily incorporate uracil opposite to adenine.
evidence: This is a statement about the consequences of dUTPase inhibition, drawing from established knowledge.

claim: Several anticancer drugs target the de novo thymidylate synthesis pathway via thymidylate synthase inhibition to perturb the tightly regulated dUTP/dTTP ratio, eventually triggering thymineless cell death.
source: Similarly, several anticancer drugs (such as 5-fluorouracil (5-FU), 5-fluoro-2'-deoxyuridine (5FdUR), capecitabine, methotrexate, raltitrexed (RTX), pemetrexed) target the de novo thymidylate synthesis pathway via thymidylate synthase inhibition to perturb the tightly regulated dUTP/dTTP ratio, eventually triggering thymineless cell death (Blackledge, 1998; Requena et al., 2016; Wilson et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Blackledge, 1998; Requena et al., 2016; Wilson et al., 2014.

claim: Massive uracil misincorporation, hyperactivity of the repair process and/or stalling of the replication fork are all suggested to be involved in the thymineless cell death mechanism.
source: Although the exact molecular mechanism is not yet fully understood, massive uracil misincorporation, hyperactivity of the repair process and/or stalling of the replication fork are all suggested to be involved in the process (Khodursky et al., 2015; Ostrer et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Khodursky et al., 2015; Ostrer et al., 2015.

claim: UNG has been suggested to play a key role in the thymineless cell death mechanism.
source: UNG has been suggested to play a key role in this mechanism, as being responsible for the initiating step in uracil removal that may lead to futile cycles if the cellular dUTP/dTTP ratio is elevated.
evidence: This is a statement about the proposed role of UNG, drawing from established knowledge and speculation.

claim: UGI expression does not affect either the cytotoxicity, or the DNA damage and cell cycle response upon RTX and 5FdUR treatment.
source: It has already been shown that UGI expression does not affect either the cytotoxicity, or the DNA damage and cell cycle response upon RTX and 5FdUR treatment (Luo et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Luo et al., 2008.

claim: A U-DNA sensor was designed from an inactive mutant of human UNG2 that was successfully applied in semi-quantitative dot blot analysis and direct immunocytochemistry.
source: Previously, we designed a uracil-DNA (U-DNA) sensor tailored from an inactive mutant of human UNG2 that was successfully applied in semi-quantitative dot blot analysis and direct immunocytochemistry (Róna et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Róna et al., 2016.

claim: Immunoprecipitation led to elevated uracil levels in enriched U-DNA samples compared to input DNA in case of both 5FdUR and RTX treated, UGI-expressing HCT116 samples.
source: Immunoprecipitation led to elevated uracil levels in enriched U-DNA samples compared to input DNA in case of both 5FdUR (5FdUR_UGI) and RTX (RTX_UGI) treated, UGI-expressing HCT116 samples.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the dot blot assay shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Drug treatment led to significantly elevated uracil levels in HCT116 cells either transiently or stably expressing UGI (~400 uracil moieties/million for 5FdUR and ~700 uracil moieties/million for RTX) as compared to non-treated cells (~2–5 uracil moieties/million).
source: Drug treatment led to significantly elevated uracil levels in HCT116 cells either transiently or stably expressing UGI (~400 uracil moieties/million for 5FdUR and ~700 uracil moieties/million for RTX) as compared to non-treated (NT) cells (~2–5 uracil moieties/million).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C with statistical analysis (p=0.002).

claim: Drug treatment resulted in even higher U-DNA content (~900 uracil moieties/million for 5FdUR and ~950 uracil moieties/million for RTX) in MMR proficient cells as compared to MMR deficient cells.
source: Drug treatment resulted in even higher U-DNA content (~900 uracil moieties/million for 5FdUR and ~950 uracil moieties/million for RTX) as compared to MMR deficient cells.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D with statistical analysis (p=0.005).

claim: U-DNA-IP led to 4.5 fold enrichment of the uracil-containing spike-in DNA compared to the uracil-free spike-in as determined by qPCR.
source: In these samples U-DNA-IP led to 4.5 fold enrichment of the uracil-containing spike-in DNA compared to the uracil-free spike-in as determined by qPCR.
evidence: This is a control experiment demonstrating the specificity of the U-DNA-IP method.

claim: Pull-down with empty anti-FLAG beads not containing the U-DNA sensor resulted in negligible amount of DNA (less than 5%).
source: Specificity of U-DNA immunoprecipitation is also underlined by the fact that pull-down with empty anti-FLAG beads not containing the U-DNA sensor (i.e. negative control) resulted in negligible amount of DNA (less than 5%, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, see also Supplementary file 1-table 1).
evidence: This is a negative control experiment demonstrating the specificity of the U-DNA-IP method.

claim: Subtracting control signals will not affect the detected uracil distribution pattern regardless if the sample was drug-treated or not.
source: We demonstrated that subtracting such control signals (for details see Supplementary file 1) will not affect the detected uracil distribution pattern regardless if the sample was drug-treated or not (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B–C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B–C.

claim: UGI expression did not cause any observable change on cell cycle progression.
source: We demonstrated that UGI expression did not cause any observable change either on cell cycle progression (Figure 5, and Luo et al., 2008) or uracil distribution pattern (Figure 3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5 and supported by citation to Luo et al., 2008.

claim: UGI expression did not cause any observable change on uracil distribution pattern.
source: We demonstrated that UGI expression did not cause any observable change either on cell cycle progression (Figure 5, and Luo et al., 2008) or uracil distribution pattern (Figure 3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3.

claim: The genomic uracil pattern is much more influenced by MMR proficiency in case of the 5FdUR treatment than in case of the RTX treatment.
source: We found that the genomic uracil pattern is much more influenced by MMR proficiency in case of the 5FdUR treatment than in case of the RTX treatment (Figure 3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3.

claim: Broad regions of uracil enriched genomic segments were detected with non-random distribution patterns.
source: The genomic uracil distribution patterns either in non-treated or in drug-treated cells are found to be non-random: broad regions of uracil enriched genomic segments were detected.
evidence: This is based on the U-DNA-Seq data analysis.

claim: In drug-treated cells, broad segments showed the highest correlation with ChIP-seq-based patterns published for predominantly euchromatin and facultative heterochromatin markers.
source: In drug-treated cells, these broad segments showed the highest correlation with ChIP-seq-based patterns published for predominantly euchromatin and facultative heterochromatin markers (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A–B through GIGGLE search and genome segmentation analysis.

claim: The drug treatment induced U-DNA pattern is more similar to the early replicating segments, whereas U-DNA distribution in non-treated cells shows simultaneous association with both heterochromatin markers and late replicating regions.
source: Accordingly, we report that the drug treatment induced U-DNA pattern is more similar to the early replicating segments, whereas U-DNA distribution in non-treated (wild type and UGI-expressing) cells shows simultaneous association with both heterochromatin markers and late replicating regions (Figure 4C–D, also supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C–D and Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: MMR proficiency leads to a major decrease in the correlation with early replication timing in case of the 5FdUR treated sample.
source: It has to be noted that MMR proficiency leads to a major decrease in the correlation with early replication timing in case of the 5FdUR treated sample (Figure 4C–D), and a smaller decrease in the correlation with transcriptionally active regions in case of both treatments (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C–D.

claim: In the non-treated cells, where the level of genomic uracil is low, uracil is preferentially located in the constitutive heterochromatin.
source: Taken together, in the non-treated cells, where the level of genomic uracil is low, we show that uracil is preferentially located in the constitutive heterochromatin, which can be explained by the fact that heterochromatin is generally highly condensed and thus less accessible for DNA repair and replicative DNA synthesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the U-DNA-Seq data analysis and correlation with genomic features.

claim: Drug treatments perturb the cellular nucleotide pool, and consequently highly increase the rate of thymine replacing uracil misincorporation events overwriting the background uracil pattern of non-treated cells' genome.
source: However, drug (5FdUR or RTX) treatments perturb the cellular nucleotide pool, and consequently highly increase the rate of thymine replacing uracil misincorporation events overwriting the background uracil pattern of non-treated cells' genome.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed data based on known mechanisms of drug action.

claim: Uracil pattern showed the highest correlation with the features linked to DNA synthesis involved in either replication, or transcription-coupled DNA repair, or epigenetic reprogramming.
source: Importantly, we found that uracil pattern showed the highest correlation with the features (early replication, active promoters and DNase hypersensitive sites, and CpG islands) linked exactly to these processes (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C.

claim: In MMR proficient drug-treated samples higher U-DNA content was measured as compared to the MMR deficient ones.
source: This is further supported by the fact that in MMR proficient drug-treated samples higher U-DNA content was measured as compared to the MMR deficient ones (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–D.

claim: The observation in MMR proficient cells might be explained by either longer segments synthesized during the MMR process, or the less tight control on cell cycle arrest allowing more extended replicative synthesis.
source: This observation in MMR proficient cells might be explained by either longer segments synthesized during the MMR process (Bowen et al., 2013), or the less tight control on cell cycle arrest (Figure 5) allowing more extended replicative synthesis.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data, with citation to Bowen et al., 2013 and reference to Figure 5.

claim: Under normal conditions, localization of human genomic uracils can be associated with the heterochromatic regions which is in agreement with the recent study by Shu et al., 2018.
source: Our data showing that under normal conditions, that is in lack of drug treatment, localization of human genomic uracils can be associated with the heterochromatic regions which is in agreement with the recent study by Shu et al., 2018.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the U-DNA-Seq data analysis and comparison with published data.

claim: The heterochromatic localization of uracil may reflect less efficient DNA repair in the heterochromatin.
source: We propose that this pattern may reflect less efficient DNA repair in the heterochromatin.
evidence: This is a proposed explanation for the observed pattern.

claim: Mutation rate within the later replicating heterochromatin is markedly increased.
source: In accordance, it was shown that mutation rate within the later replicating heterochromatin is markedly increased (Stamatoyannopoulos et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Stamatoyannopoulos et al., 2009.

claim: Uracil distribution in bacterial and yeast genomes was found to be mostly excluded from the earliest as well as from the latest replicating segments.
source: Interestingly, uracil distribution in bacterial and yeast genomes was found to be mostly excluded from the earliest as well as from the latest replicating segments (Bryan et al., 2014), suggesting a partially different pattern as compared to what is observed in human cells.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Bryan et al., 2014.

claim: In yeast cells, transcription coupled repair synthesis might result in elevated uracil incorporation into actively transcribed regions under normal conditions.
source: In yeast cells it was also shown that transcription coupled repair synthesis might result in elevated uracil incorporation into actively transcribed regions under normal conditions (Kim and Jinks-Robertson, 2009; Owiti et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Kim and Jinks-Robertson, 2009; Owiti et al., 2018.

claim: Both yeast and bacteria show major differences in both mechanisms of dNTP pool regulation and the set of available UDGs, as they do not encode the SMUG1 enzyme which is an important backup of the UNG2 in human.
source: However, both yeast and bacteria show major differences in both mechanisms of dNTP pool regulation (Mathews, 2014) and the set of available UDGs, as they do not encode the SMUG1 enzyme which is an important backup of the UNG2 in human (Elateri et al., 2003; Kavli et al., 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Mathews, 2014; Elateri et al., 2003; Kavli et al., 2002.

claim: The antifolate or nucleotide-based thymidylate synthase inhibitors are known to lead to cell cycle arrest.
source: The antifolate or nucleotide-based thymidylate synthase inhibitors, such as 5-FU, RTX or 5FdUR are known to lead to cell cycle arrest, as it is confirmed in our experimental system (Figure 5) and is also reflected in the detected uracil-DNA pattern that strongly correlates with the early replicating segments in case of both drug treatments.
evidence: This is confirmed by the cell cycle analysis shown in Figure 5 and is established knowledge.

claim: The two drugs caused similar, but not equivalent uracil-DNA pattern.
source: The two drugs caused similar, but not equivalent uracil-DNA pattern.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the U-DNA-Seq data analysis.

claim: The correlations with the H3K36me3 marker as well as with the early replicating segments are both markedly stronger with the RTX treated sample as compared to the 5FdUR treated sample.
source: On the one hand, the correlations with the H3K36me3 marker as well as with the early replicating segments are both markedly stronger with the RTX treated sample as compared to the 5FdUR treated sample (Figure 4).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4.

claim: The correlation of uracil accumulation with the H3K27me3 marker and with the CpG islands is stronger in the 5FdUR treated sample.
source: On the other hand, the correlation of uracil accumulation with the H3K27me3 marker and with the CpG islands is stronger in the 5FdUR treated sample.
evidence: This is based on the correlation analysis of U-DNA-Seq data.

claim: The MMR status has markedly different influence on the resulting U-DNA pattern in case of the two drugs.
source: Moreover, the MMR status has markedly different influence on the resulting U-DNA pattern in case of the two drugs (Figures 3–4).
evidence: This is shown in Figures 3–4.

claim: Both drugs inhibit thymidylate synthase thereby facilitating dUMP incorporation into DNA, while the nucleotide analogue 5FdUR also leads to direct incorporation of 5-fluorodeoxyuridine monophosphate (FdUP) into the DNA.
source: Still, it is well-known that both drugs inhibit thymidylate synthase thereby facilitating dUMP incorporation into DNA, while the nucleotide analogue 5FdUR also leads to direct incorporation of 5-fluorodeoxyuridine monophosphate (FdUP) into the DNA (Longley et al., 2003; Pettersen et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Longley et al., 2003; Pettersen et al., 2011.

claim: The U-DNA-Seq method detects both uracil and also fluorouracil within the DNA, since the UNG enzyme binds to fluorouracil as well.
source: It should be noted that our method detects both uracil and also fluorouracil within the DNA, since the UNG enzyme binds to fluorouracil as well (Pettersen et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Pettersen et al., 2011.

claim: The 5FdUR treatment was shown to cause an S-phase arrest in the second cycle.
source: The 5FdUR treatment was shown to cause an S-phase arrest in the second cycle (Huehls et al., 2016; Yan et al., 2016), while the actual time point of cell cycle arrest upon RTX treatment is still controversial (Blackledge, 1998; Ding et al., 2019; Zhao et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Huehls et al., 2016; Yan et al., 2016.

claim: The actual time point of cell cycle arrest upon RTX treatment is still controversial.
source: The 5FdUR treatment was shown to cause an S-phase arrest in the second cycle (Huehls et al., 2016; Yan et al., 2016), while the actual time point of cell cycle arrest upon RTX treatment is still controversial (Blackledge, 1998; Ding et al., 2019; Zhao et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Blackledge, 1998; Ding et al., 2019; Zhao et al., 2016.

claim: Slightly altered cell cycle distribution patterns were detected in case of the two drug treatments, which were differently influenced by the MMR status.
source: Similarly, we also detected slightly altered cell cycle distribution patterns in case of the two drug treatments, which were differently influenced by the MMR status (Figure 5).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5.

claim: In case of the 5FdUR treatment, MMR proficiency seems to lead to a weaker S-phase arrest.
source: In case of the 5FdUR treatment, MMR proficiency seems to lead to a weaker S-phase arrest.
evidence: This is an observation based on the cell cycle analysis.

claim: Equally induced DNA damage response (reported by γH2AX) was detected upon both drug treatments.
source: However, equally induced DNA damage response (reported by γH2AX) was detected upon both drug treatments (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Treatment with the antifolate pemetrexed in UNG -/- human colon cancer cells led to preferential enrichment of double-strand breaks (DSBs) within highly accessible euchromatic regions, like transcription factor binding sites, origins of replication, DNase hypersensitivity regions and CpG islands.
source: Consistently with our observations, Weeks et al recently showed that treatment with the antifolate pemetrexed in UNG -/- human colon cancer cells led to preferential enrichment of double-strand breaks (DSBs) within highly accessible euchromatic regions, like transcription factor binding sites, origins of replication, DNase hypersensitivity regions and CpG islands (Weeks et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Weeks et al., 2014.

claim: The FLAG-ΔUNG-SNAP sensor construct and the optimized staining method were successfully applied in confocal and super-resolution (STED or dSTORM) microscopies.
source: The FLAG-ΔUNG-SNAP sensor construct and the optimized staining method presented here were successfully applied in confocal and super-resolution (STED or dSTORM) microscopies (see Figures 6–8).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figures 6–8.

claim: Using dSTORM super-resolution microscopy, significant correlation of genomic uracil with both H3K36me3 and H3K27me3 histone markers was confirmed in drug-treated (5FdUR or RTX), UGI-expressing cells.
source: Using dSTORM super-resolution microscopy we could confirm significant correlation of genomic uracil with both selected histone markers in drug-treated (5FdUR or RTX), UGI-expressing cells (Figure 8).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8 with statistical analysis (p < 0.0001).

claim: H3K36me3 was shown to associate with actively transcribed genes.
source: H3K36me3 was shown to associate with actively transcribed genes (Becker et al., 2017; Hyun et al., 2017; Pfister et al., 2014), while H3K27me3 is the most cited marker for facultative heterochromatin (Becker et al., 2017; Saksouk et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Becker et al., 2017; Hyun et al., 2017; Pfister et al., 2014.

claim: H3K27me3 is the most cited marker for facultative heterochromatin.
source: H3K36me3 was shown to associate with actively transcribed genes (Becker et al., 2017; Hyun et al., 2017; Pfister et al., 2014), while H3K27me3 is the most cited marker for facultative heterochromatin (Becker et al., 2017; Saksouk et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Becker et al., 2017; Saksouk et al., 2015.

claim: H3K27me3 shows even stronger colocalization with the U-DNA pattern in case of the RTX treated sample as compared to the 5FdUR treated one, which might be indicative for RTX treatment induced chromatin remodeling at least regarding this histone modification.
source: Strikingly, we found that H3K27me3 shows even stronger colocalization with the U-DNA pattern in case of the RTX treated sample as compared to the 5FdUR treated one, which might be indicative for RTX treatment induced chromatin remodeling at least regarding this histone modification.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the colocalization data.

claim: RTX treatment does not cause general chromatin remodeling, but may rather confine to certain factors.
source: With the ChIP-seq experiment for H3K36me3 performed on both RTX treated and non-treated cells, we demonstrated that such treatment-induced chromatin remodeling is not a general phenomenon, but may rather confine to certain factors (Figure 4A–B, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4A–B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Co-staining of the selected histone markers and the genomic uracil in drug-treated cells via dSTORM reinforced the association between uracil occurrence and transcriptionally active regions.
source: In summary, co-staining of the selected histone markers and the genomic uracil in drug-treated cells via dSTORM reinforced the association between uracil occurrence and transcriptionally active regions.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the dSTORM colocalization data.

claim: Uracil accumulation may play a more decisive role in genomic instability than the induced uracil-excision repair.
source: It has been argued that uracil accumulation may play a more decisive role in genomic instability than the induced uracil-excision repair (Huehls et al., 2016; Yan et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Huehls et al., 2016; Yan et al., 2016.
